notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2200.tlg00427.opp-gr: §2 'κατὰ τῶν μων' is corrupt; 'against the [laws]' (νόμων) is conjectural, and the sense of ἐμέλλησε here is uncertain. §4 last sentence is corrupt ('τὰ δὲ δία ... τῶν οἰκιῶν'); rendered as if 'the children' (παιδία) and 'fear of [their] households/masters'; sense uncertain. §5 'τὸ δος' read as 'the reality' (τὸ δ' ἔργον or similar). §6 'ποιητής' ('composer', ironic) may be corrupt. §7 'κράτη' read as Σωκράτη. §8 'λογεῖς' read as λέγεις. §12 'κτεῖς' read as ἄχθῃ ('you are annoyed'); 'οἱ' read as οἱ δ'. §13 'τουργηκὼς' read as λελειτουργηκὼς. Letoius and Eumolpius appear to be earlier governors; Euploius, Charidemus, Antiochus, Pherenicus, Hermeias and Coccus are as named in the text.

18: the text is defective in several places; translated as restored: 'ἀποδεδώκεις <ἂν> αὐτόν, [νῦν] δὲ', '[τοι]ούτων λόγων'. In 'κατηγορεῖ τῶν ...σμένων' the participle is incomplete (perhaps 'those who had been wronged' or 'those who had demanded [him back]'), so it is left as [...]. 20: 'ὀνήσοντα ...δονίους' is defective; the people meant (…donians, perhaps Chalcedonians or Macedonians) cannot be identified with confidence. 21: 'the shell turned over' is a proverb for a sudden reversal. 24: the edition's apparatus (cf. Diogen. III 54 …; 'τὸν στενωπὸν]') has intruded into the text and is omitted; after 'ὡς' something seems lost before 'ἀγαθὸς ἐκεῖνος'. 27: 'ἀρτοπόπνω' is read as ἀρτοποιῶν/ἀρτοπωλῶν, 'bakers'. 30: 'μισθὸς παρὰ μὲν οὔπω πληγέντων τούτου … τοῦ μὴ χαλεπώτερα' is elliptical or corrupt; the sense given is conjectural. 'σὲ δὲ των' is read as τούτων. 'λογισμοῖς' is taken as the public accounts.

32: 'Phoenix' (Φοίνικα) could instead mean 'a Phoenician councillor'; taken as a name. 'Belts' (ζώνας) refers to imperial service posts, entry into which freed men from curial duties. 43: πευθήν, 'informer', probably an agens in rebus. 'τῶν μένων' looks corrupt (perhaps for ἀρχομένων, 'subjects', or μενόντων); rendered 'those who remain'. 38: the sense of the last clause about the letter is unclear.

nodes.text: FIRST [SPEECH] AGAINST ICARIUS.

Since, in praising [him], I saw fit [to speak of] those deeds of Icarius that belonged to the better portion, I think it proper not to keep silent about the worse ones either. For in this way justice would be preserved on both counts, the one set of deeds receiving praise and the other accusation, and at the same time I should be shown by this to be least of all a flatterer, if the places where he has done wrong are also told. I do not know of any of the others who have written such things who has done this. Rather, the man they once praised as good they go on praising, even if the facts urge them to do the opposite, as though they themselves would have to give account for what those men did improperly.

2. Now, that Icarius took [bribes], or meant to, against the [laws], not even those who hate him intensely would say; nor that he was a slave to women's beauty, nor that he spent his nights in long sleep. But another sickness had seized his soul: suspicion towards most of what was well said, and an inability to find what was needed himself, together with a rejection of the best advice, because he thought the adviser said what he said in order to arrange something to his own advantage.

I told him this myself many times, rebuking him, and he smiled and did not deny it, as if he were doing something good. For this reason, when a bridge which carries most supplies into the city had been cut by a great flood, and our food supply was in a bad way, I said that this misfortune needed the spirit of Letoius, who had quickly set right many such things; but he insulted my advice with silence, supposing that my concern was not that the city should be well served but that the man [should be]. Thallus the doctor used to visit him, adding the counsels of his judgement to the services of his art. He shut his doors on him, without convicting him of anything, but having persuaded himself that he was being betrayed.

About the grooms whose work is with the racehorses I spoke and told the truth: that previously they had prevented the savage thefts committed by others now through their own humane ones. For whatever they stole, they gave back to the owners, taking from them, willingly given, a little, enough to cover their lunch; and no other thief was about, for fear of these men. 'But now', I said, 'they have been stopped' (and I named the man who had stopped them, and how, and why), 'and everything is full of criminals who know no moderation, who prey on the age that is easiest to deceive. And the children, fear of their households drives to the river, and it, having drowned them, [carries them] to the sea.'

So while I was trying to restore so great a benefit to the city, I heard frigid words: that it was shameful to make [men] thieves. He feared the word, but did not reckon with the reality; he kept so great a harm in place, afraid of syllables. And how much better it would have been to be more pained by the deaths caused by the thefts than to fear thefts close to a game, at which some have even laughed? If, when you were pressed by a most grievous disease, one of the gods told you that he would drive it out with another, very light and with nothing dangerous in it, would you think even then that accepting the lesser was among the most absurd of things? So sensible is Icarius, and so able, partly by his own thinking, partly by heeding another, to make his subjects happy!

6. Now hear another thing. When the famine had filled our city with beggars, some of whom had left the countryside since they had not even grass, at least in winter, while others had abandoned their own cities, and some help for them had been found from the court through the humanity of Eumolpius, he was urged by me to do the same, for I said it was dreadful if, at such a time, the greater office should appear worse than the lesser. On hearing this, the noble composer gave that wonderful reply: he said that all such people are hated by the gods.

Then will you say that the rich are loved by the gods? Yet among these are pirates, and those on land who resemble them, who possess the money of those they have butchered. And in general we shall find the more unjust the more prosperous. So you are saying nothing other than that the gods love the more wicked, and that every poor man, or anyone unfortunate in some other respect, is their enemy. Consider then where you place your father when you philosophise like this, and before your father many men renowned for philosophy and other virtues, unless you would also say that Socrates, who died by hemlock, was hated by the gods.

And indeed, that the cities have suffered loss in the number of their people through famine and plague is plain to everyone; but if they are perishing through the hatred of the gods, you would reasonably rejoice over them. Do you say, then, that you rejoice at the loss suffered by the cities?

9. I do not know what a man would have to do to be thought good by you, if you will regard slanders as trustworthy but suspect praises. What do I have in view in saying this? Euploius calls this man his son, and he calls him father. A letter once came from Euploius, wishing Charidemus to receive full consideration and, where it is permitted, to have some advantage. This man took the letter and even took away from him some of what he had before, so that he ignored him more than previously, thinking himself wronged by the letter. For he believed it had come from this man, and that it belonged not so much to the one who sent it as to the one who persuaded him to send it.

I, then, did not write, but in person I told him to invite Antiochus into the court, a man who says what he thinks, has flattered no one, and knows how to speak. But when I said this and much else besides, and lied in nothing, he said, as though he would die on the spot if [Antiochus] merely peeped in, that he would endure anything sooner than this. And yet, if what you did in Antiochus' case is good, it ought to have been applied to all; but if the opposite, why did he not come in and sit [there], being far better in character than those who have held commands, and no worse than us who teach the young?

But, I suppose, what comes from me and the doctor is terribly suspect, while what comes from the attendants is above suspicion, and if the soldier says anything, you add the deed. That is why bakers are under the lash every day. For the one who has not courted Pherenicus with much money is guilty about the weight, and what happened with one loaf (and many things might cause this) is extended to all, and Pherenicus' word must prevail. And they hold me to blame, who persuaded them to come down from the mountains.

12. I am also under reproach among the councillors, because on the most splendid New Year's day one man was kissed, though the law grants this to all. You are annoyed at being hated, but you do the things from which this would come about. For [choosing] one instead of all had this effect: the one felt no gratitude at receiving what was customary, while the others were indignant at being deprived of what was owed them.

And why should I spend time on lesser matters, when I have [to tell of] blows to a councillor that gave the doctors trouble, so that at first they could not even say whether he would live? For a man who was in poverty because of the chariot races, and who had performed public services before and was still performing them, was beaten on the back, though old laws forbid it, and the one recently enacted forbids it, paying the penalty not for wrongs he himself had done, but for those of certain people who in the baths acclaimed the name of Coccus. How then is it not unjust that they were the cause of the anger, but that Hermeias reaped its consequences? And yet we know that not even Coccus, who dared a great deal, dared this; however mad he was in other things, in this at least he was sane, and did not outrage the council with blows.

14. Do you want me to tell you also about the fine guard, the soldiers at the gates, whose pretext was to prevent the farmer from taking out more than two loaves, but whose real business was to sell the right of export to the farmers? For from those from whom they got nothing they did not allow even as much as it was lawful to take out, while those who paid could take out as much as they liked. Neglecting what they ought to do, they did whatever would increase their own [gains]. And you, either you knew this and were not indignant, or you did not know and so did wrong; the one is negligence, the other betrayal.

15. And what defence could he have about the evils that are common to those in the city and those in the countryside? I mean the business of the rubbish, which he allowed to be carried out on other people's donkeys, when he ought to have compelled [people to use] their own. How heavy the burden is, the tears of those dragged into this show; that it is unjust, he himself testifies by having forbidden it. For when he had just come to us and found this widespread, he at once stopped such loads, greatly benefiting the market by this.

But he, who regarded the practice as terrible and harmful to the city, who claimed to be ashamed on behalf of those who had granted such favours, and who said they did not even deserve to be called governors, was himself the one granting these favours. And if [he had done it] in summer, he would be on a level with them; but since [he did it] in winter too, he is more unjust, since mud is [worse] than rubbish: the one is mud from the start, while the other becomes it even as it is carried, the rains doing this. So when the same man both forbids the same thing to be done and allows it to be done, has he not condemned himself for having granted wicked favours?

17. Look also, if you like, at another change, by which this man, who used to avoid luncheons and drinking, where he would have had to offend even the most powerful, went wherever he was invited, not examining who it was who invited him; anyone was worthy who could claim mention of a post on the staff. So those who used to bring this charge against others were no longer in the same position.

18. Not even this favour is a fine one, but the one I shall speak of is much worse. Where now is the bald man posted? Among those under you. And where did the law post him? Among those under Eumolpius, the law acting justly in bringing back the runaway. How then did this come about? If you had obeyed the law, you would have handed him back; [but now] you grant to people you know of the favour of leaving him where he was, you who came on behalf of the laws and would not have tolerated [such] words. And he, made bold by the promises, shouts and makes you stop, and accuses those [...], and seems to speak justly, and wins against you with you as judge; and freed from the fears he used to fear, he goes through the city making others afraid, while those who achieved this for him look on beaming at his beaming face.

19. I think, then, that the same people, by similar arguments, have also prevailed in the matter of the small sum of money, which was hunted down by the excellent Cleinias as it lay at the harbour awaiting the voyage to Carthage; it made our city weaker, and would have made it stronger if it had been returned and brought up [to us]. We kept thinking that we would have it the next day, but the city has not recovered the money even now.

And as for the profits from this to the man who claims to help Seleucia but does what he knows will benefit the [...]donians, do you think the people of Antioch are ignorant of these things, or are not angry knowing them, or need seers to learn who received this favour, which has brought you blame, and nothing else (for I must tell the truth), but to them gain as well, towards which they gape all the time without fear?

You took better counsel in your first days, when you drove away the father of your assessor, and were planning how to expel the assessor himself, since more letters than was proper were coming in and going out, some from the one, some from the other; and you had glory both from what you did and from what you intended. Then, when the shell turned over, as they say, both became your dearest friends. The door stood open to all letters, and it stood open to the father. People thought you had found what you ought to do, but had not dared [to do it] out of some fear.

So you filled the deserted alley of the father with people, and he whom his little garden used to feed on vegetables alone now has luxury from every quarter. Of the gifts, some are a recompense, some an inducement. The neighbours look on in amazement. He sells the letters to Phoenicia, and if anyone needs something from your office, once he has courted that man he is confident of the outcome.

It was he too who showed off this novelty. Callippus, whom he made out to the governor to be sensible and sober and able to set right some of the city's affairs, the man who drinks below the foothills from dawn with many looking on, then dances, then drinks, then dances again, who thinks it a great thing if he reconciles prostitutes who are fighting: this is the man who persuaded you, this is the one who deceived you.

And you, hearing that he was good, at once believed, passing over a test that is formidable at revealing a man's nature. What test is this? His care for his own affairs. And you did not ask those from whom you would have learned the truth: has this man, even if he did not add to his inherited wealth, at least preserved it? You would have heard that everything had been sold, everything spent, everything gone through his privates and his belly. Do not put up with those who say he used up his estate on public services. For this is the man who abused even the emperor's generosity, recovering his lands and selling them on the same day, and very nearly eating up the whole price on the spot. Or was he performing public services for the city then too? Will you count Lais in place of Zeus?

This man, then, who stripped himself of what he had inherited, who borrowed much and repaid little, who became the cause of death for many market traders by promising to pay them the price of what he ate and never paying, which drove the men even to long for death, this man you make master of so many peoples, and you are not afraid that the emperor may learn that the market goods have been put in Callippus' hands by your decree?

So you were persuaded that the bad man is good; but you must learn what some strangers who came recently said. When I was speaking rather well of you, as I used to do, 'But we,' they said, 'are neighbours of your city; we respect you, but Callippus wipes out these praises of yours. For being bad he would not have pleased a good man, if Icarius were good.' That he is bad was shown by the daily beatings, by their number and their severity, and by their extending to everything.

And yet he had received from you [only] a part, that concerning the bakers, but he had given himself everything else, laid his hands on everything, and ruined everyone, beating them senselessly, calling to account matters for which there had never been any audits, and ordering in writing what was impossible, that the shopkeepers sell each item for less than they had bought it, which is better called madness than folly. And yet if someone asked him, 'Why, after hiding at home all the rest of the time, do you now see fit to flash like lightning, when even if you had done this before, it would have been time for you to stop?', what would he answer, except that before he had no one who would trust him, but now he has found one?

Whom then do you think the wronged curse? I would not say, but it is plain to all. For this Callippus is not even one man; each of his slaves is too, and they are many. So these too are Callippuses, who call passers-by to the goods for sale and tell them to grab them, saying it is allowed, while the seller stands stunned, his hands clasped, lamenting in silence, so as not to suffer something worse.

And the greater part of this tragedy is [the work] of the man who has his daughter, lives with him and is joined to him in all his villainies, indicating to the wronged that something must be given to him too. And they give to both. Or where do you think the penniless Callippus [gets the means] to be a splendid host, trying to show up that Roman as nothing, starting with the pheasants themselves?

30. All these things, Icarius, are thefts, or, if you like, payment: from those not yet beaten, for this [not happening], and from those who have suffered it, for [suffering] nothing worse. But none of [these things] moves you to anger, because of those who sing spells over you, who were great in the governorship of Coccus and are great now, though we did not hope for this, but that those who were great then would be small, and those who were outraged then would be in honour. But you have kept for each group what they had before, for the one their power, for the other what they had then; and you set the former over the accounts, giving them opportunities for gain, while the latter, who could not praise Coccus, see their speech thrust out by your expression, even if they say the best things.

And this is the prize for Eurybatus the councillor for the labours he endured over the inscriptions on the walls, removing some and writing others in their place, when those ordered to do this were not at all willing, and when there were some dangers in this for the one compelling them. And what is still worse, those whom you thought owed you a penalty because, to please another, they plotted against your interests, these you made masters of audits that can make them rich. How is this not lunacy, when the man who deserves punishment is well treated, and the one to whom gratitude was owed is badly treated?

And where is the fine thing in this, that speeches are made for the city by Harmodius, the city's advocate, and you hear none of it, but think that he is talking nonsense? Nor is it fine that the people, when they invite you to the shows, do not even hear that you will come, and this when you are going to come. From whom did you learn that silence benefits a governorship, even when affairs demand speech? For my part, I think one must avoid going beyond the mean in either direction. But you fix your eyes and give the impression of [preparing] a speech, yet say nothing whatever. And the man who has said something to you goes away having said what he said in vain.

33. 'But you have helped oratory by the honours [you give it].' And the honours are lending your ears to all who wish. And what honour is this, that those who are not equal obtain equal things? For the man who has judged worse and better worthy of the same things has harmed just honours by unjust ones. For what is fittingly given is no longer as great as it would be if it stopped with the deserving.

For by this reasoning we shall make the crown at Pisa common to victors and vanquished, and the prizes at the trophies common to those who have done best and those who have done the enemy no harm at all. What pleasure, then, is there for those who have rightly received their rewards, along with those who have not rightly been adorned with the same? These men will certainly be very eager to toil for such a fruit! So from this the athlete becomes worse, and the soldier becomes worse, as they shun a toil that brings them nothing more.

35. How, then, has he himself increased the stock of oratory for us by this lack of restraint about recitals? For I think it has been brought low, since anyone who wishes finds a day for his own drivel; but you call this love of listening and zeal for oratory, and you seem to me to be someone who, after the lyre of Apollo, would go to [the tunes] of these beggars in the taverns and expect to be called a lover of the Muses.

Then do you not see that if this is fine for you, it is also fine, when a cobbler or a smith invites you to dinner, to accept, and to go and recline and dine, and to be the same at every table? Or shall we shun the one because of the station of those inviting, but welcome the tediousness of these? Do you not know the laughter that arose at each of those who spoke, when men of that sort came to give displays, and you submitted yourself to those who offered such stuff, which, as I hear, you yourself laughed at when you had left? Yet it is much better to push away those who pester you than to be insulted by what is said and then to find fault with oratory.

37. Furthermore, you heard some, but did not deign [to hear] others who were in no way inferior to them, so that the reproach of inconsistency was added to you as well. How then did this come about? You would have taken your seat again, but those whose nods you follow granted to those who spoke that these others should not speak. And at a thing over which anyone who was well disposed to you would hide his face: everything displayed was at once up for request, and as much as was laughed at; and many feet [ran] at the man who had just finished, not letting him breathe, exacting, throttling, as though you would not even endure to take your lunch before receiving [it]. So, by what you did, you robbed those whom you found in good repute of the repute they had. A wonderful champion of oratory you have come to us, who drove mad even those who knew how to keep silent the rest of the time, and made them seek to have what till then they did not think fit [to seek].

38. Then you say that everything is small to you compared with me, and that you think you see your own father in me. But this father, when because of the severity of an illness he had had a vein cut and could not get sleep and needed much comfort, this man did not visit through any of his friends, nor even of his servants. Nor again, when being escorted off, did he say anything of the sort to any of my associates, as would have befitted one who had often said those things. But when you had gone away to Phoenicia, you sent a letter censuring our city, which did the work of those who try to restrain wrongdoers, but could not bind them.

39. And indeed in this too you fight with yourself: for you hate our city as not hating Coccus, while you yourself all but bowed down to him. So far did you go beyond custom in your attentions, teaching Berytus to remember nothing of what it had suffered. And to others this seemed something astonishing, but for me it confirmed an expectation long held, since you were both honouring and preserving his measures and wanting them to stay fixed, so that I do not know what more he would have had from his own father, if that man had been the one to take over the governorship.

Accordingly all those holding accusations in their hands are speechless, though they are so many that they would make the size of the courtroom seem small. But the fear of incurring some further harm if they did not keep silent has stopped their mouths. And those many wounds have remained undying because of the good Icarius.

He will say he has heard these things from the powerful men in the palace. But in saying this, he names those for whose sake he has done wrong, whereas it would have been better for him to be able to say that he has done no wrong. I would say, then, that that is their concern; but the man who heard [this] ought to have spoken a simple word: 'I am sent to stop what is unjust, not to make it strong.' But I hear that he has gone through every injustice, and to me it is finer to be a private man than to govern like this. What terrible thing would you have suffered by coming into office and undoing as many of Coccus' measures as was possible? 'This would have made the term of my office short.' Very well. But praised, at least. And a governorship of one day that has justice is better than to have occupied the seat all one's life without it.

But the man who excuses himself to us by his grief over what was done to Germanus showed Phoenix, a councillor who had willingly remained in performing his public service, almost dead from blows. On what charge? That he did not come with others. But what if he alone was able to do this, and the task was too great for the poverty of the others? What if they were fleeing Emesa, no longer a city? What if they were hiding while staying? But you do not weep for a city of such quality and size that has been ruined, nor do you restore, if not all, at least some one part of the good things it once had; yet you beat the one man against the laws and proclaim to all: 'Do not perform public services, do not take part in civic life, do not sit on the council; go off to belts, greater or lesser.'

43. And with what words you honoured the city of Antiochus too! The man who carried your kindly greeting was Uranius the informer, and he heard you saying very earnestly—these were the words—that you hated everyone, one after another. Oh, the folly! You shout what you ought to hide, and you blurt out such things against you as could have stayed unnoticed, and you teach so great a city to hate you. For surely the city will do the same. And indeed it is a governor's part to treat his subjects well, but those whom one hates one necessarily treats not well but badly. So you treat some of those who remain badly—and who they are, let that be left aside for now.

44. Say the same, then, to those who meet you too: that you hate each one and would gladly learn that they were all dead. And you could, if you wished, add to the people the land and buildings and draught animals and springs, for thus your hatred will be more splendid; and to your household, too, when you return home, along with your other talk about your governorship, let this be included as well, and, if you like, first.
